title: The HERITAGE Family Study
goal: Explain what HERITAGE found about how much VO₂max gains vary and run in families, what a heritability of 47% does and doesn't mean, and the study's limits.

steps.title: A training study built on families
steps.text:
Why do two people on the same plan improve by different amounts? The HERITAGE Family Study was built to ask that.

It recruited whole families: two parents and at least two grown-up children, all sedentary. In the 1999 analysis, 481 white adults from 98 families trained on a cycle ergometer for 20 weeks, and [VO2max](g:vo2max) was tested twice before and twice after [[c:her-n]]. Everyone did the same plan, three supervised sessions a week, from 30 min at the heart rate of 55% of VO₂max up to 50 min at 75% for the last 6 weeks [[c:her-protocol]].

Why families? Relatives share [genes](g:gene). If the gain clusters in families ([familial aggregation](g:familial-aggregation)), something families share shapes [trainability](g:trainability).

claims.text: HERITAGE trained 481 sedentary adults from 98 two-generation families for 20 weeks, with VO₂max tested twice before and twice after.

evidence.quote: A total of 481 sedentary adult Caucasians from 98 two-generation families was exercise trained for 20 wk and was tested for VO(2max) on a cycle ergometer twice before and twice after the training program.

claims.text: The programme was standardised: 3 sessions a week, from 30 min at the heart rate of 55% of VO₂max to 50 min at 75% in the last 6 weeks.

evidence.quote: The intensity or duration of the training sessions was increased every 2 wk, until subjects were working at the HR associated with 75% of baseline V̇O2max for 50 min during the last 6 wk

steps.title: Same plan, very different gains
steps.text:
On average VO₂max rose by about 400 mL·min⁻¹. But the spread was huge: some people gained little or nothing, others more than 1.0 L·min⁻¹ [[c:her-mean]]. A later summary gives the mean as 384 mL·min⁻¹ with a [standard deviation](g:standard-deviation) of 202 [[c:her-sd]].

Even in the most alike subgroup, young men aged 17–35, the mean gain was 15.7% with an SD of 8.7%. Most gained 10–20%, some nothing, some 40–60%: a skewed spread with a long tail of big gainers [[c:her-young]].

Remember the setting: same plan, same relative intensity, every session supervised, and only people who did at least 57 of the 60 sessions counted. The spread isn't explained by skipped sessions [[c:her-supervised]].

claims.text: The mean VO₂max gain was about 400 mL·min⁻¹, ranging from little or none to over 1.0 L·min⁻¹.

evidence.quote: The mean increase in VO(2max) reached approximately 400 ml/min, but there was considerable heterogeneity in responsiveness, with some individuals experiencing little or no gain, whereas others gained >1.0 l/min.

claims.text: The mean gain was 384 mL·min⁻¹ with an SD of 202 mL·min⁻¹.

evidence.quote: The mean gain in V̇O2max was 384 mL O2 (SD, 202).

claims.text: In young men aged 17–35 the gain was 15.7% ± 8.7%, from none to 40–60%.

evidence.quote: The mean gain reached 15.7%, with SD of 8.7%. Even though most tended to improve by about 10% to 20%, the range of responses is wide, with some experiencing no gain and others improving by 40% to 60%, as illustrated by the skewed distribution.

claims.text: All sessions were supervised on site, and post-training results counted only participants who completed at least 57 of the 60 sessions.

evidence.quote: All training sessions were supervised on-site by trained personnel to ensure that the equipment was working properly, and the participants were compliant with the protocol.
Posttraining numbers include only the subjects who were classified as completers having completed at least 57 (95%) of the 60 exercise training sessions.

steps.title: Reading a mean and an SD
steps.problem: Suppose a training study reports a mean VO₂max gain of 400 mL·min⁻¹ with an SD of 200 mL·min⁻¹. Roughly where do two thirds of people lie, and how unusual is a gain of zero?
steps: About two thirds of values lie within one SD of the mean: 400 − 200 = 200 and 400 + 200 = 600 mL·min⁻¹.
A gain of 0 is (0 − 400) ÷ 200 = −2 SD from the mean. In a bell-shaped spread about 2–3% of people lie further than 2 SD below the mean.
In 481 people that is roughly 10 people with no gain at all, even on a plan that works on average. (Real gains are skewed, so treat this as a rough guide.)

steps.title: 47%: what heritability means
steps.text:
The gain varied 2.5 times more between families than within them. The best-fitting model gave a maximal [heritability](g:heritability) of 47% for the VO₂max response [[c:her-h2-response]]. Before training, VO₂max itself (429 people, 86 families) had a maximal heritability of at least 50% [[c:her-h2-base]].

Read 47% carefully. It means that about half of the *differences between people* in this group, on this plan, went with family. It does not mean that 47% of your own gain comes from your genes: one person's gain can't be split that way.

It also belongs to the setting. When everyone trains the same, more of the remaining spread can come from genes; give people very different plans and the same genes explain a smaller share.

claims.text: VO₂max gains varied 2.5 times more between families than within them, with a maximal heritability of 47%.

evidence.quote: An ANOVA revealed that there was 2.5 times more variance between families than within families in the VO(2max) response variance.

With the use of a model-fitting procedure, the most parsimonious models yielded a maximal heritability estimate of 47% for the VO(2max) response, which was adjusted for age and sex with a maternal transmission of 28% in one of the models.

claims.text: In the sedentary state, VO₂max had a maximal heritability of at least 50%.

evidence.quote: Maximal heritability estimates were at least 50%, a value inflated to an undetermined degree by nongenetic factors.

steps.title: What HERITAGE does not show
steps.text:
Three cautions.

**Families share more than genes.** Spouses, who share no genes, had alike VO₂max too, so home life plays a part, and the authors say the heritability is inflated by non-genetic factors to an unknown degree [[c:her-shared-env]].

**No control group.** The money went to more families instead, which made later analyses harder; without one, a study can't separate training effects from changes that would have happened anyway [[c:her-no-control]]. Without one, the spread of changes can't be cleanly split into true differences and test noise (*Noise, worthwhile changes and non-responders*). Testing twice at each end reduces the noise but doesn't remove it.

**One dose.** Only one standard dose was tested [[c:her-one-dose]]. A small gain on 20 weeks of moderate cycling says nothing about a bigger or harder plan. And the 47% comes from sedentary white adults.

claims.text: Spouse correlations show that shared environment adds to family resemblance in VO₂max, so heritability estimates are inflated by non-genetic factors.

evidence.quote: Spouse, sibling, and parent-offspring correlations were significant, suggesting that both genetic and environmental factors contribute to the familial resemblance for VO2max.
Maximal heritability estimates were at least 50%, a value inflated to an undetermined degree by nongenetic factors.

claims.text: HERITAGE had no control group: the money went to more families, and the gap limits secondary analyses, since designs without a control group cannot separate training effects from changes that would have happened anyway.

evidence.quote: The lack of a control group became a challenge when the HERITAGE resource was used in secondary analyses.
Indeed, the consensus was that the funding available would be better devoted to reaching a larger sample size of families and participants in both ethnic groups than to add a control group.

Designs without a control group (or control condition) (ie, designs 1, 2 and 3) cannot isolate changes due to treatment (eg, exercise training) from changes that would have occurred in the absence of treatment.

claims.text: HERITAGE tested only one standardised dose of exercise.

evidence.quote: Other limitations include that only one standardized dose of exercise was tested, children and older adults were not incorporated into the study

points: HERITAGE gave 481 sedentary adults from 98 families the same supervised 20-week cycling plan, testing VO₂max twice before and after.
The mean gain was about 400 mL·min⁻¹ (SD about 200), from little or none to over 1 L·min⁻¹.
Gains clustered in families: maximal heritability 47% for the gain, at least 50% for VO₂max before training.
Heritability describes the spread in one group on one plan; it can't say how much of one person's gain is genetic.
Shared home life inflates family estimates, there was no control group, and one moderate dose can't show who can't improve.

variants.stem: Why did HERITAGE recruit whole families instead of unrelated volunteers?

options.text: To see whether the training gain clusters in families
options.why: Right: comparing the spread between and within families shows whether response runs in families, and so whether genes (or family life) play a part.

options.text: To have relatives act as an untrained control group
options.why: There was no control group: every participant trained.

options.text: Because relatives train together and so stick to the plan
options.why: Every session was supervised on site; adherence wasn't the reason for families.

options.text: To remove the effect of genes on the results
options.why: The opposite: families were chosen to measure the effect of genes, not to remove it.

variants.stem: In HERITAGE, about how much did VO₂max rise on average after 20 weeks of training?

options.text: About 400 mL·min⁻¹
options.why: Right: about 400 mL·min⁻¹ (384 in the later summary).

options.text: About 1.0 L·min⁻¹
options.why: That was the top of the range, reached only by the biggest gainers.

options.text: About 40 mL·min⁻¹
options.why: That is ten times too small: it would be within test noise.

options.text: About 4 L·min⁻¹
options.why: That is a whole VO₂max of a fit adult, not a gain.

variants.stem: A summary of HERITAGE gives the mean VO₂max gain as 384 mL·min⁻¹ with an SD of 202 mL·min⁻¹. Between which values do roughly two thirds of people lie?

options.text: 182 to 586 mL·min⁻¹
options.why: Right: mean ± 1 SD = 384 − 202 to 384 + 202.

options.text: 384 to 586 mL·min⁻¹
options.why: This adds the SD on one side only; the band goes both ways from the mean.

options.text: −20 to 788 mL·min⁻¹
options.why: That is ± 2 SD (384 ± 404), which holds about 95% of people, not two thirds.

options.text: 202 to 384 mL·min⁻¹
options.why: This treats the SD as the lowest value instead of a distance from the mean.

variants.solution: Two thirds lie within 1 SD of the mean: 384 − 202 = 182 and 384 + 202 = 586 mL·min⁻¹. The real spread is skewed, so this is approximate.

variants.stem: In HERITAGE's young white men, VO₂max rose by 15.7% on average, with an SD of 8.7%. Between which gains do roughly two thirds of them lie?

options.why: This adds the SD on one side only.
That is ± 2 SD, about 95% of people.
This treats the SD as the lowest gain.

variants.stem: A 12-week running study reports a mean VO₂max gain of 5.0 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ with an SD of 2.5. Between which gains do roughly two thirds of runners lie?

options.text: 2.5 to 7.5 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
5.0 to 7.5 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
options.why: This adds the SD on one side only.

options.text: 0 to 10.0 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
options.why: That is ± 2 SD, about 95% of runners.

options.text: 2.5 to 5.0 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
options.why: This takes the SD down from the mean only.

variants.stem: A cyclist reads about HERITAGE and says: "So 47% of my VO₂max gain is decided by my genes." What is the best correction?

options.text: 47% describes differences between people in that group, not a share of one person's gain
options.why: Right: heritability is about the spread in a group on a given plan; it can't be applied to one person's gain.

options.text: The figure is right but only for VO₂max before training
options.why: 47% was the heritability of the gain; VO₂max before training was at least 50%.

options.text: Genes decide 53% of the gain, since 47% is the share due to training
options.why: Heritability isn't a split between genes and training for one person.

options.text: 47% means his gain will be about 47% smaller than average
options.why: Heritability says nothing about the size of a gain.

variants.stem: Study A gives 200 runners the same supervised plan. Study B lets 200 runners train anywhere from 2 to 8 hours a week. Both estimate the heritability of the VO₂max gain. What do you expect?

options.text: Lower heritability in B, because training differences add non-genetic spread
options.why: Right: heritability is a share of the spread; when training varies, more of the spread comes from training, so genes explain a smaller share.

options.text: The same in both, since runners' genes don't change between studies
options.why: The genes are the same, but heritability is a share of the spread, which depends on the setting.

options.text: Higher heritability in B, since more training reveals the genes
options.why: More varied training adds non-genetic spread, so genes take a smaller share of it.

options.text: Heritability can't be estimated when training is supervised
options.why: HERITAGE was supervised and estimated it fine.

variants.stem: A blog uses HERITAGE's spread of VO₂max changes to claim that a fixed share of people are 'non-responders'. What most limits that claim?

options.text: There was no control group to show how much of the spread is test noise
options.why: Right: without a control group (or repeat testing), true differences can't be separated from day-to-day noise and regression to the mean.

options.text: The sample was too small to see a spread
options.why: 481 people from 98 families is large for a training study.

options.text: Nobody checked that people did their sessions
options.why: Every session was supervised on site.

options.text: VO₂max was measured only once at each end
options.why: It was measured twice before and twice after, which reduces noise.

variants.stem: In HERITAGE, husbands' and wives' VO₂max before training were also alike, although spouses share no genes. What does that mean for the 'at least 50%' heritability?

options.text: Shared home life also makes families alike, so the estimate is likely too high
options.why: Right: the authors say the estimate is inflated by non-genetic factors to an unknown degree.

options.text: It proves VO₂max has nothing to do with genes
options.why: Parents and children were alike too, and the data fit a genetic part; spouses show only that environment adds to it.

options.text: Spouses must be related, so the estimate is too low
options.why: Spouses aren't blood relatives; their likeness comes from shared life (and choosing alike partners).

options.text: It has no bearing: spouses aren't used to estimate heritability
options.why: Spouse likeness is how a family study detects the share of shared environment.

variants.stem: A triathlete did a HERITAGE-style plan: 20 weeks, three moderate 50-minute sessions a week. Her VO₂max barely moved. What is the soundest conclusion?

options.text: She responded little to this dose; a different or bigger plan may work
options.why: Right: HERITAGE tested one moderate dose, so a low gain on it says nothing about other plans.

options.text: Her genes make her a non-responder to endurance training
options.why: One plan and one pair of test results can't show that; a later lesson shows that higher doses can turn non-response around.

options.text: Her heritability for VO₂max is low
options.why: Heritability belongs to a group, not to one person.

options.text: She should stop training for VO₂max and focus on economy
options.why: Too early: a low response to one moderate plan is weak evidence about her trainability.
